sentences.text: Alder had 13 readmissions. The reference clinic, given the same patients, expects 8.
Is that a real difference? Or could a clinic exactly like the reference have had 13, just by luck?
To answer, we need to see what luck looks like.
We'll start with Dune, because Dune has only 12 patients, and we can watch every one of them.
Dune had 7 readmissions against 4.8 expected: the highest raw rate in the cast. So make a guess. Is Dune unusual?
Welcome back to Model in Motion.
Today: unequal coins.
Suppose Dune were exactly like the reference. Then each patient is a coin.
For the six lower-risk patients, it comes up readmitted 18% of the time. For the six higher-risk patients, 62%.
Flip all twelve and count. Three readmissions.
Flip again: five. And again: three.
Do it two thousand times, and the counts pile up around 4.8.
That pile is what luck looks like, for a clinic like the reference with Dune's patients.
We don't actually have to flip anything. The pile can be worked out exactly, one coin at a time.
Each new coin splits every bar in two. One part stays where it is: no readmission. The other moves one step to the right.
After twelve coins, the chance of exactly 5 is 26%. Of 6, 19%. Of 7, 9%. And of 8 or more, 4%.
Dune's count was 7. For a clinic just like the reference, the chance of 7 or more is 13%.
Two refinements. Counts move in whole steps, so we take only half of the bar at 7 itself. That brings it to 8%.
And a clinic can surprise us in either direction, so we double it: 16%.
That is the p-value. About one time in six, luck alone does this. Dune is not flagged.
Now Alder. Thirty coins: 24 at 18%, and 6 at 62%. The pile centres on 8.
Alder's 13 sits far out in the tail. The chance of 13 or more is two and a half percent, and the p-value is 3.5%.
That is below the usual 5% line. Alder is flagged: more readmissions than luck comfortably explains.
So the clinic with the highest raw rate is not flagged, and Alder is. Twelve patients leave a lot of room for luck. Thirty leave less.
For the others: Birch, 45%. Cedar, 99%. And Elm, 11%, which is simply its whole bar at zero.
Why insist that the coins are unequal? Swap Alder's thirty for thirty identical coins with the same average.
The pile gets wider. The p-value rises from 3.5% to 5.2%, and Alder slips under the bar.
Mixed coins vary less than identical ones. Use the right pile, and the test is sharper.
So far we built the pile at the reference. But we can build it at any gamma, and ask where Alder's 13 stops being surprising.
Slide the gamma up, and the pile slides right. Between minus 1.46 and plus 0.13, thirteen is unremarkable.
That is Alder's exact 95% interval. The reference, at minus 1.52, lies just outside it: the same verdict as the flag.
Carried through the rising curve from Episode 11, Alder's ratio lies between 1.04 and 2.26. Dune's, between 0.82 and 2.04, which includes 1.
Does the test keep its promise? We built fifty crowds in which every provider truly equals the reference, and tested all ten thousand.
It flagged 4.8%, against the 5% it promises.
Two cautions. The test treats the dial and the reference as known.
And a p-value is not the chance that the clinic is ordinary. It is the chance of a count like this, if it were.
Let's gather it up.
If a clinic were like the reference, each patient would be a coin with a chance of their own.
The count's whole distribution can be worked out exactly, and the tail beyond what was observed gives the p-value.
Turned inside out, the same test gives an interval.
Exact is satisfying, but it takes work. Are there quicker ways to nearly the same answer?
Next time: three shortcuts.
This has been Model in Motion. Thanks for following the story.
